text: Gerald Okafor knocked on the side door on Saturday morning holding a rolled-up survey map. He explained that he wanted to put up a six-foot cedar fence along the line between the two lots, starting at the corner of the garage and running back to the alley. He spread the map on the hood of the car and pointed to the iron pins the surveyor had marked in 2009. According to the drawing, the line ran about eight inches west of the old row of hedges. He said the fence company would set the posts on his side of the pins, so the hedges could stay where they were. The installation would take two days, and the crew would need access through the side yard for the post-hole auger. He asked whether Tuesday and Wednesday of the following week would work, and he left a copy of the quote, which listed the materials, the gate hardware, and a note that the finished side would face out.

I measured the yard myself before the meeting with my neighbor, Ines Carvalho. Using a hundred-foot tape, I ran from the front sidewalk marker to the back corner and got ninety-four feet, two inches. Ines came over at four with a printout from the county assessor's website showing the parcel outlines. We compared the numbers, and they matched within an inch. She wanted a vinyl fence, white, five feet tall, with a single gate near the compost bins. The city required a permit for anything over four feet, so she had already filled out the application. It asked for a sketch with the setback from the sidewalk, which had to be at least three feet. We walked the line together and placed orange flags every ten feet. She said the utility locating service would come Thursday to paint the gas and water lines before any digging. I wrote the dates on the calendar in the kitchen.

Tomasz Wierzbicki had been planning the fence since spring. He printed the municipal code section on residential boundaries and read it at the kitchen table: fences on a shared line required written consent from both owners, or else had to sit entirely within one property. He drafted a short letter to the household next door, describing the material as galvanized chain link with green vinyl coating, four feet high. He included a diagram with the post spacing at eight feet and a note that he would cover the full cost. On Monday he walked the letter over and handed it to the woman who answered, Mrs. Adeyemi, who read it on the porch. She asked whether the posts would be set in concrete, and he said yes, eighteen inches deep. She asked for a few days to look at the plat herself. He left his phone number written at the bottom of the page.

The fence contractor arrived at eight with a truck and a trailer stacked with pressure-treated pine. My neighbor, Darnell Whitfield, had hired the company, and he and I had agreed on the plan a month earlier over the hedge. The foreman, a man in a gray jacket, walked the property line with a can of marking paint and sprayed small white dots where each post would go. He checked each spot against the survey stakes with a laser level. Darnell came out with two cups of coffee and handed me one. The foreman explained the sequence: holes first, then posts set in quick-dry concrete, then the rails the next morning, and the pickets last. The old wire fence would be pulled out and hauled away. I moved my recycling bins and the garden hose reel to the other side of the house so the crew would have room for the auger.

Priya Raghunathan found the note taped to her front door after work. It was from the owners of the house to the north, the Lindqvists, and said they planned to install a wooden privacy fence along the property line and would like to discuss it. The note gave a phone number and suggested a time on Sunday afternoon. Priya pulled the closing documents for her house out of the filing cabinet and found the survey, which showed the lot as a rectangle sixty feet wide. The north line was marked by two pins, one near the street and one near the back shed. On Sunday she walked over at two o'clock. Mr. Lindqvist had a sample board of stained fir propped against the porch rail. He explained that the fence would be six feet tall and that the posts would go on their side. Priya asked about the drainage swale, and he said there would be a two-inch gap at the bottom.

I called the county records office on Tuesday because my neighbor, Hamid Sorouri, had asked me to confirm where the line was before he ordered fence panels. The clerk told me the most recent recorded survey for my parcel was from 1987 and could be requested as a copy for four dollars. I filled out the request form online and had it in my email by Thursday. The drawing showed the boundary running in a straight line from the curb to a concrete monument at the rear. Hamid and I found the monument under some ivy by the back corner. It was a small square post with a brass cap stamped with the surveyor's license number. He took a photo of it and sent it to the fence company. They said they would offset the fence six inches toward his side to stay clear of the line, and they would deliver the panels the following Monday.

Mbali Nkosi's neighbor, an older man named Clifford Haines, stopped her at the mailbox. He said the dogs from the rental two doors down had been cutting across both yards, and he wanted to put up a fence between his lot and hers to keep them out. He proposed a four-foot split-rail fence with wire mesh attached on the inside. He had already priced it at the hardware store: twenty-two rails, twelve posts, two rolls of mesh, and a box of staples. He suggested splitting the materials cost, which came to roughly six hundred dollars, and said he would do the labor himself with his son-in-law over a weekend. Mbali asked whether there would be a gate between the two yards. Clifford said he could add one near the back, by the vegetable beds. She said she would check her budget and get back to him by the end of the week.

I hired a licensed surveyor before agreeing to anything about the fence. My neighbor, Rosalind Achterberg, had proposed a masonry wall along the side of the property, and that kind of structure is hard to move later. The surveyor, a woman with a tripod and a data collector, spent about three hours on the site. She located the original corner pins and set two new wooden stakes with pink ribbon where the pins had been buried too deep to see. She explained that the line was about a foot east of where both of us had assumed. That meant the strip of lawn by my driveway was technically on Rosalind's side. I sent the stamped survey to Rosalind by email that evening. She replied the next morning that the wall would be built along the corrected line, and she attached a drawing from her mason showing a footing two feet deep and a height of five feet.

Kenji Matsuda spent the evening reading the homeowners association guidelines. Section 4.2 covered fences: maximum height of six feet in back yards, four feet in front yards, and only wood, wrought iron, or black aluminum allowed. Any new fence required an architectural review form, signed by the adjacent owners, to be submitted at least thirty days before construction. His neighbor, Beatriz Montalvo, had mentioned the idea of a fence the week before while they were both out pulling weeds. Kenji printed the form and filled in the section describing the project. He wrote down the length of the line, one hundred and twelve feet, and attached a photo of the style Beatriz had shown him on her phone, a horizontal slat design in dark brown. The next morning he walked the form over. Beatriz signed on the line marked adjacent owner, and they agreed she would drop it at the association office on Friday.

The meeting with my neighbor took place at the folding table in his garage. Osvaldo Reyes had laid out three brochures from fence companies, each with a quote stapled to the front. The cheapest option was a vinyl picket fence at forty-one dollars per linear foot installed. The second was cedar at thirty-six dollars per foot, and the third was ornamental steel at fifty-eight. He had drawn the yard on graph paper, with each square representing two feet. The fence would run the full length of our shared line and stop eight feet short of the sidewalk, as required by the city's corner visibility rule. I asked about maintenance on the cedar, and he said it would need a sealant every three years. We decided on the cedar. He said he would call the company in the morning to schedule the estimate visit and send me the contract to look over before signing.

Arturo Benedetti lived on a corner lot, and his neighbor to the east, Moana Kealoha, had asked about building a fence along their side yards. They met at the property line one evening with a ball of string and two stakes. Moana tied the string to the first stake at the front and walked it back to the second at the rear, pulling it taut. The line passed about a foot from the trunk of the maple tree that sat between the houses. Arturo noted that the roots would make digging difficult near the trunk. Moana suggested shifting one post to the left and using a longer rail section to span the root zone. They agreed to ask the fence company whether a ten-foot span would hold without sagging. Arturo took a photo of the string line from the street side so they would have a reference when the estimator came.

I received a certified letter from the property management company that owns the duplex next to my house. The letter, signed by a representative named Yusuf Demirci, stated that the owners planned to install a fence along the shared property boundary as part of a renovation. It described the fence as six-foot board-on-board pine, with posts placed eighteen inches inside the owner's side of the line. The letter included a copy of the survey and a schedule: post installation the week of the fourteenth, panel installation the week after. It asked me to remove any personal items within three feet of the line before work began. I walked the side yard and found two flower pots, a bench, and a coiled hose that needed to be moved. I also called the number on the letter to ask about trimming the hedge. Yusuf said the crew would trim only the branches extending over the line.

Halima Abdi found the envelope in her mailbox on Thursday, addressed in printed type from the building's management office. Inside was a single page titled Notice of Lease Renewal. It stated that her current twelve-month lease would end on the last day of August and offered two options: a new twelve-month lease at a monthly rent of fourteen hundred and twenty dollars, or a month-to-month arrangement at fifteen hundred and ten. The letter asked her to return the signed form by July fifteenth. A second paragraph explained that the building would be switching to a new online payment portal in September, and that tenants would receive login instructions by email. Halima put the letter on the counter next to her keys. She opened her laptop and compared the new rent figure to her current one, which was thirteen hundred and seventy-five. Then she checked her calendar for the July deadline and set a reminder.

The letter from my landlord was short. It said that the water to the building would be shut off on Wednesday between nine in the morning and two in the afternoon while a plumber replaced a section of the main line in the basement. It also mentioned that, per section eleven of the lease, the landlord was giving the required forty-eight hours of notice before entering units, because the plumber needed to check the shutoff valves under each kitchen sink. The landlord, Mr. Feinberg, signed it at the bottom with his phone number. I read the lease clause to make sure it matched, and it did. I cleared out the cabinet under the sink that night, moving the cleaning supplies and the trash bags to the hallway closet. I also filled a large pot and two pitchers with water to use for cooking on Wednesday and left the spare key with the building's superintendent.

Rafael Quintero sat down at his desk with the letter from his landlord and a pen. The letter explained that the property had been sold and that a new management company, Ridgeway Residential, would take over on the first of the month. All terms of the existing lease would remain in effect until its expiration date. Rent should now be paid to the new company, either by check mailed to an address in the next county or through their website. The security deposit, the letter said, had been transferred in full to the new owner and would be held under the same terms. Rafael highlighted the new mailing address and the website. He wrote the date of the transfer on a sticky note and attached it to his copy of the lease. Then he logged in to his bank's website and updated the payee information for the recurring rent payment, changing the name and the address.

I opened the landlord's letter while standing in the stairwell of my building. It was a reminder that my lease required renters insurance with at least one hundred thousand dollars in liability coverage, and that the management office had no proof of a current policy on file for my unit. The letter asked me to send a copy of the declarations page within fourteen days. I had bought the policy the previous year through an online insurer. When I got upstairs, I logged into the account and found that the policy had renewed automatically in March. I downloaded the declarations page as a PDF, checked that the liability limit was listed, and emailed it to the address at the bottom of the letter, which belonged to an office assistant named Wanjiru Kamau. She replied that afternoon and confirmed that the document had been added to my tenant file.

Svetlana Morozova lived in a third-floor unit of a converted mill building. The letter from her landlord arrived in a brown envelope with the company logo in the corner. It announced that the building would be repainted in May, including the hallways, stairwells, and exterior trim. The schedule listed which floors would be painted on which days, and her floor was assigned to the second week. The letter asked tenants to keep doormats and shoe racks inside their units during that period and noted that the stairwell on the north side would be closed for two days while it dried. Elevator access would remain available. At the end, the letter mentioned that tenants could request a specific paint color for their front doors from a list of four options. Svetlana checked the list, chose the dark green, and wrote her unit number on the attached reply slip.

When I got home from my shift, there was an envelope taped to my door. It was from the landlord, Mrs. Pellegrino, and it said she was planning to install new smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in every unit to comply with an updated state regulation. The work would be done by an electrician on the twenty-second, between ten and noon. The letter stated that the new detectors would be hardwired with battery backup, and that the old battery-only units would be removed. It also listed the lease section that permitted entry for safety repairs with twenty-four hours of notice. I took a picture of the letter and put it in the folder on my phone where I keep documents about the apartment. On the morning of the twenty-second, I moved the bookshelf in the hallway about a foot so the electrician could reach the ceiling with his ladder.

Cyrus Tehrani received the letter by email as a PDF attachment. The landlord, a small company run by two brothers, was informing tenants of a change in the trash and recycling schedule. Starting the next month, pickup would move from Tuesday to Friday, and the dumpster enclosure would get a new lock with a four-digit code. The code was printed in bold in the second paragraph. The letter also reminded tenants that cardboard boxes needed to be broken down flat and that large items such as furniture required a separate pickup request through the city. Cyrus read the attachment and saved it to a folder labeled Apartment. He wrote the dumpster code on a small piece of masking tape and stuck it on the inside of his kitchen cabinet door. He then moved the reminder on his phone for taking out the recycling from Monday night to Thursday night.

My landlord sent a letter explaining that the parking arrangement for the building was changing. The lot behind the building had twelve spaces, and up until now they had been first come, first served. Starting in October, each unit would be assigned one numbered space, and a parking permit sticker would be required on the rear windshield. Any car without a sticker, the letter said, could be towed by the company listed at the bottom. Units with a second car could rent a space in a lot across the street for sixty dollars a month. The stickers would be available at the office on weekdays between nine and five, and tenants needed to bring their vehicle registration. I went to the office on my lunch break the following Monday. The office manager, Thandiwe Mokoena, checked my registration against the lease, handed me a sticker for space number seven, and showed me where it was on a printed map.

Ivar Halvorsen read the letter from his landlord in the lobby while waiting for the elevator. It stated that the heating system would be switched from the old oil boiler to a new natural gas system over the summer. As part of the project, workers would need to enter each unit for about an hour to replace the radiator valves. The letter included a sign-up sheet with available time slots. It also noted that heating costs, which were currently included in the rent, would remain included after the switch. At the bottom, there was a contact name for questions, a project coordinator named Leticia Bramble. Ivar took the letter upstairs and looked at his work calendar. Most of the slots were on weekday mornings. He picked one on a Friday at eight, since he worked from home on Fridays, and slid the completed sheet under the office door on his way out that evening.

The letter came in a plain white envelope with my name and unit number written by hand. My landlord, an older man who owned only this one building, wrote that he had noticed a bicycle locked to the railing on the front steps and wanted to remind tenants that the lease prohibited storing items in common areas. He explained that the fire marshal had cited the building for a blocked egress the previous year. He said he had cleared out a section of the basement and installed a rack with room for eight bicycles. A key to the basement door was available from him, with a ten-dollar deposit. The bicycle was mine. I went downstairs and unlocked it from the railing, then knocked on his door on the first floor. He handed me a brass key on a ring with a paper tag, and I paid the deposit in cash. He wrote me a receipt on a small notepad.

Noor Haddad sat at her kitchen table with the landlord's letter and a copy of her lease side by side. The letter said that the landlord intended to raise the pet fee from twenty-five to forty dollars per month at the next renewal, and that all pets needed updated vaccination records on file. Noor had a cat, eleven years old, named Biscuit. She checked the lease and found the pet addendum on page nine. It stated that pet fees could be adjusted at renewal with sixty days of written notice. The letter was dated sixty-three days before her renewal date, so the notice period was satisfied. She pulled Biscuit's vaccination certificate from a folder of veterinary papers and saw that the rabies booster was due next month. She called the clinic and booked an appointment for the following Saturday, then put the letter and the certificate together in an envelope to drop off after the visit.

The landlord's letter was about the laundry room. I read it out loud to my roommate, Benedikt Krause, while he was making toast. The two coin-operated washers and the single dryer in the basement were being replaced with four newer machines that accepted payment through a mobile app or a reloadable card. The card could be purchased at a kiosk next to the machines. The price per wash would go from two dollars and fifty cents to two seventy-five, and drying would stay at two dollars. The laundry room hours would also change, from seven in the morning to ten at night. The installation was scheduled for the following Thursday, and the room would be closed that day. Benedikt said he would do his laundry on Wednesday to get ahead of it. I downloaded the app and created an account so we would have it ready.

The departures board at Gate 14 changed the status of flight 2271 to Delayed and listed a new time of 4:40, two hours later than scheduled. Matteo Ricci checked the airline app on his phone, which showed the same time and a short note that the aircraft was arriving late from Denver. He had a carry-on bag and a backpack, and he had already eaten lunch before security. He found a seat near a charging station and plugged in his phone. A gate agent made an announcement that passengers with connections in Chicago should come to the desk to review their options. Matteo's itinerary was a direct flight, so he stayed where he was. He opened his laptop and finished the expense report he had been putting off, then emailed the hotel to let them know he would check in around nine. The hotel replied that the room would be held under the guarantee on his card.

My flight to Lisbon was delayed by three hours because of a mechanical inspection. The gate agent, a man whose name tag said Olumide, read the announcement twice over the speaker, first in English and then in Portuguese. He explained that a part on the left engine needed to be checked by maintenance before departure, and that the airline would issue meal vouchers worth fifteen dollars to every passenger on the flight. I lined up at the desk and received the voucher, a small printed slip with a barcode. It was valid at any of the food outlets in Terminal B. I walked to a sandwich shop near Gate 22 and bought a turkey sandwich and a bottle of water, which came to fourteen dollars and sixty cents. When I came back, the board showed a new estimated departure time of 7:15. I sent a message to my sister in Lisbon with the updated arrival time.

Ayesha Siddiqui was at the counter of the regional airport when the agent told her the morning flight to the hub city had been delayed. Fog had kept the incoming aircraft on the ground at its origin. The new departure was estimated for 11:30, which would cause her to miss her connection to Toronto. The agent typed for several minutes and then offered two alternatives: a later connection that afternoon that would arrive in Toronto at 9:50 in the evening, or a different routing through Montreal arriving at 8:15. Ayesha asked which option had more open seats on the second leg. The agent said the Montreal routing had twelve available and the other had three. She chose Montreal. The agent printed two new boarding passes and retagged her checked suitcase with a new routing label. Ayesha placed the boarding passes in the front pocket of her bag and walked toward the security line.

I was flying home after a work conference, and the email from the airline arrived while I was still in the taxi. It said my flight had been delayed by ninety minutes due to air traffic control restrictions at the destination airport. The email included a link to rebook for free if I wanted to change to a different flight on the same day. I opened the link and saw that the only other flight that day left earlier, at 1:05, which I could not make. I kept my original booking. At the airport, I checked my bag at the kiosk, which printed the tag and a receipt, and walked through security in about fifteen minutes. The gate was at the far end of Concourse C. I sat by the window and watched a ground crew load catering carts into a plane at the next gate. A colleague named Marisol Echeverría, who was on the same flight, sat down a few seats away.

Gunnar Eriksson's flight was showing a delay of forty minutes when he arrived at the gate, and then it moved to an hour and a half. The airline posted a reason on the screen: crew rest requirements. The first officer scheduled for the flight had come in on a late arrival the night before and needed the mandatory number of hours off before working again. Gunnar read the explanation on the airline's website, which described the federal rules on flight crew duty time. He had a book with him, a history of shipbuilding in the Baltic, and he read two chapters. At one point he walked to the newsstand and bought a pack of gum and a bottle of sparkling water. When he returned, a new crew had arrived at the gate and was going through the jet bridge door. The gate agent began boarding by group number twenty minutes later.

The airline sent a text message to my phone at 5:52 in the morning stating that flight 418 to Phoenix was now scheduled to depart at 9:10 instead of 7:30. I had already set my alarm for 5:00, so I was awake and dressed. I used the extra time to make a full breakfast: two eggs, toast, and coffee. My partner, Chidi Okonkwo, drove me to the airport at 7:20, which was about an hour later than we had originally planned. The drop-off lane was busy, with cars lined up past the third door. I went inside, printed my boarding pass at a kiosk, and checked the departure board, which still listed 9:10. Security took twenty minutes. At the gate, I found an outlet near the window and charged my phone. The board updated once more, to 9:25, and the gate agent announced that the aircraft was being refueled.

Lucía Fernández was traveling with her two children, ages six and nine, when the flight was delayed. The gate agent announced that thunderstorms near the destination had led to a ground stop, and no flights could depart for that city until it was lifted. The estimated new departure time was two hours later. Lucía took the children to the airport play area near Gate 30, which had a small climbing structure and benches along the wall. She bought two bags of pretzels and a carton of apple juice at a kiosk. Her older son had a tablet with a downloaded movie, and her daughter used a coloring book and a set of crayons from Lucía's bag. Every half hour, Lucía checked the app on her phone. At 4:10, it showed that the ground stop had been lifted and that boarding would begin at 4:35. She gathered their things and walked back to the gate.

The delay was announced at 3:15. The flight to Nairobi, which I was taking for a two-week project, would now depart at 11:40 at night instead of 6:20 in the evening. The gate agent said the airline was arranging a substitute aircraft because the original one had a hydraulic issue. Since the delay was over five hours, the airline offered access to its lounge for passengers in the main cabin. I took the escalator up to the lounge and showed my boarding pass at the desk. The attendant, a woman named Yuki Tanabe, gave me a wifi password on a printed card. The lounge had a buffet with soup, rice, salad, and fruit. I took a bowl of lentil soup and found a table near a power outlet. I spent two hours reviewing the project documents and then sent an email to the team in Nairobi with my new arrival time.

Desmond Clarke had a window seat on a flight that had already boarded when the captain came on the intercom. The captain explained that a warning light had come on during the preflight checks, and maintenance was coming out to look at it. He estimated that the inspection would take about thirty minutes. The cabin crew offered water in small plastic cups. Desmond had his headphones in his bag, so he took them out and listened to a podcast about bridge engineering. Through the window, he could see a maintenance truck pull up near the wing and two technicians climb a portable ladder. After forty-five minutes, the captain announced that the issue was a faulty sensor, which had been replaced, and that they would need to complete new paperwork before departing. The plane pushed back from the gate twenty minutes after that, and Desmond checked the time on his watch: 2:55.

My flight from Seoul was delayed overnight because of a typhoon warning. The airline sent passengers to a hotel near the airport and provided a shuttle from the lower level of the terminal. I lined up with about forty other people. At the hotel desk, the receptionist checked my name against a printed list and handed me a key card for room 618, along with dinner and breakfast vouchers. The dinner was a buffet in the hotel restaurant that served rice, grilled fish, soup, and a few kinds of pickled vegetables. The airline had rebooked everyone on a flight leaving at 10:00 the next morning and posted the details on a sheet of paper at the front desk. I set my alarm for 6:30, since the shuttle back to the airport would leave at 7:15. In the morning, I ate breakfast, checked out, and got on the shuttle with a man named Florian Brandt, who was on the same flight.

Oyelaran Adebayo-Smith arrived at the airport two hours early and learned at the bag drop that his flight to Atlanta was delayed by four hours. The reason, according to the agent, was that the plane had been diverted the previous evening and was out of position. The agent said he could either wait or switch to a flight on a partner airline departing in ninety minutes. The partner flight would land at a different terminal in Atlanta, but his bag would be transferred automatically. He chose the partner flight. The agent printed a new boarding pass and a bag tag with a different airline code. Oyelaran walked to the other terminal on the moving walkway, which took about ten minutes, and went through a second security checkpoint. At the new gate, he confirmed with the gate agent that his checked bag appeared in their system. The agent turned the screen toward him and showed him the bag's tag number.

I checked the flight status page on the morning of my trip, and flight 1132 to Halifax was listed as delayed by two hours and ten minutes, with the reason given as late inbound aircraft. My connecting flight was the next day, so there was no risk to the itinerary. I left the house later than planned. At the airport, I went through security and walked to the bookstore, where I bought a crossword magazine and a pen. Then I found a seat at Gate 7, near a man named Kwabena Asante who was working on a spreadsheet. He asked whether I knew if the delay had changed again, and I told him the board showed the same time as the website. I finished three crosswords. The gate agent made a boarding announcement at 2:40, starting with passengers who needed extra time, then families, and then the groups in numerical order. I was in group four.

Eleanor Whitcombe logged into the patient portal on Tuesday evening and found a new message under Test Results. It was the lipid panel from the blood draw she had done the previous Friday. The table listed total cholesterol at 212, LDL at 131, HDL at 58, and triglycerides at 115. Each value had a reference range printed beside it, and the LDL was flagged with a small letter H. Below the table, her physician, Dr. Bhattacharya, had written a short note. She said the LDL was slightly above the target range and recommended repeating the test in six months, with a focus on diet in the meantime. She attached a two-page handout from the clinic about fiber intake and saturated fat. Eleanor printed the handout and the results and put them in the binder where she kept her medical paperwork. Then she opened her calendar and entered a reminder for the follow-up test in May.

The nurse called me at 10:15 in the morning to go over the results of my thyroid test. She introduced herself as Gwen from Dr. Lindgren's office and confirmed my date of birth. She explained that my TSH level was 6.2, which was above the normal range of 0.4 to 4.5, and that my free T4 was within the normal range. She said the doctor wanted to start me on a low dose of levothyroxine, twenty-five micrograms, taken once a day on an empty stomach. The prescription had already been sent to the pharmacy on file. She also told me to schedule a repeat blood test in eight weeks so they could check whether the dose needed to be adjusted. I wrote down the medication name and the dose on the notepad by the phone. After the call, I booked the follow-up lab appointment online for the second week of March.

Rashid Al-Mansouri sat in the exam room while the doctor scrolled through the results on a computer monitor mounted to the wall. The doctor, a man in his fifties named Dr. Kowalczyk, turned the screen so Rashid could see it. The chest X-ray from the previous week showed clear lungs, he said, with no sign of the infiltrate seen on the earlier film. The pneumonia had resolved. He pointed to the two images side by side, the old one with a hazy patch in the lower right lobe and the new one without it. He listened to Rashid's chest with a stethoscope and asked about the cough. Rashid said it had mostly stopped, except for a little in the morning. The doctor said that a lingering cough could last a few weeks after the infection cleared and that no further imaging was needed. He printed a visit summary and handed it to Rashid at the door.

I opened the envelope from the lab on the kitchen counter. It was the results of the allergy panel my doctor had ordered after I described the sneezing every April. The report listed about twenty allergens with a number next to each one, measured in kilounits per liter, and a class rating from zero to six. Most of the values were class zero. Birch pollen was class three, oak was class two, and timothy grass was class one. Dust mites, cat dander, and the food allergens were all class zero. A cover letter signed by my physician, Dr. Ferreira, said that the results were consistent with seasonal tree pollen allergy and suggested starting a nasal steroid spray two weeks before the pollen season. I looked up the regional pollen calendar online and saw that birch usually peaked in late April. I added a note to my calendar for the first of April to start the spray.

Zainab Oyelowo received a phone call from the imaging center the day after her bone density scan. The technician on the line explained that the radiologist had read the scan and sent the report to her primary care provider, but that patients could request a copy directly. Zainab asked for one by email. The report arrived an hour later. It listed T-scores for the lumbar spine and the left hip. The spine score was minus 1.4, and the hip was minus 1.1, both in the range classified as osteopenia. The report recommended calcium and vitamin D supplementation and a repeat scan in two years. Zainab looked up the terms on the website of a national health service, which explained the scale used for T-scores. She wrote a list of three questions for her next appointment: what dose of vitamin D to take, whether weight-bearing exercise would help, and whether a scan in two years was standard.

The doctor's office sent a letter with the results of my annual blood work. My glucose was 94, my A1C was 5.3 percent, and my kidney and liver values were all within the reference ranges. My vitamin D level was 22, below the recommended range of 30 to 100. The letter recommended taking two thousand international units of vitamin D3 daily. I went to the pharmacy that afternoon and found the supplements on the third aisle. There were several brands. I picked a bottle of ninety softgels that listed two thousand units per capsule. At the register, the pharmacist, a man named Arash Karimi, asked whether I took any other medications that might interact with it, and I said only a daily antihistamine. He said there was no interaction. I paid, took the bottle home, and put it in the cabinet next to the coffee mugs so I would see it every morning.

Beatrix Lindholm sat in the parking lot of the clinic and opened the results on her phone. It was the follow-up urine culture from the previous week. The report said no growth after forty-eight hours, which meant the urinary tract infection had cleared after the course of antibiotics. The previous culture, which was also visible in the portal, had shown more than one hundred thousand colony-forming units of E. coli. A note from the physician assistant, Marcus Delacroix, said no further treatment was needed and that she could follow up as needed. Beatrix tapped through the rest of the portal to check whether the referral for her physical therapy appointment had been processed. It was listed as approved, with an appointment window to be scheduled. She called the physical therapy office from the car and booked the first session for the following Thursday at eight in the morning.

The dermatologist's office called me back on a Wednesday afternoon about the biopsy from the mole on my shoulder. The medical assistant who called, whose name was Paulina, read from the pathology report. The diagnosis was a benign compound nevus, with clear margins. She explained that this meant the cells were normal and the whole mole had been removed during the procedure. No additional treatment was needed. She told me to keep the stitches covered for a few more days and to come back to have them removed on the fourteenth. She also recommended a full skin check once a year. I asked whether I could swim before the stitches came out, and she said it would be better to wait. I wrote the appointment date on the whiteboard in the hallway. Then I texted my brother, who had driven me to the biopsy, to let him know the result and the date for the stitch removal.

Sebastián Ortega went to the clinic to pick up a paper copy of his hearing test results for his employer, which required an annual audiogram for workers on the factory floor. The receptionist printed the report and placed it in a manila envelope. Sebastián looked at it in the waiting area. The chart showed two lines, one for each ear, plotted across frequencies from 250 to 8,000 hertz. Both lines stayed above the twenty-five decibel threshold until 4,000 hertz, where the left ear dropped to thirty-five. The audiologist's note said there was a mild high-frequency loss in the left ear and recommended consistent use of hearing protection rated at least NRR 29. It also suggested retesting in twelve months. Sebastián handed the envelope to the safety coordinator at work the next morning. She made a copy for his file and gave him a new box of foam earplugs with the correct rating printed on the side.

I had my eye exam on a Monday, and the results came in the form of a printed prescription the optometrist handed me at the end of the visit. My right eye was minus 2.25 with a cylinder of minus 0.50 at an axis of 180 degrees, and my left eye was minus 2.00 with no cylinder. Compared to my previous prescription from two years earlier, the right eye had changed by a quarter diopter. The optometrist, Dr. Nakagawa, said the retinal scan and the eye pressure test were normal, with pressures of fourteen in both eyes. She recommended a follow-up in two years. I took the prescription to the optical shop in the front of the building, where an optician named Ewan helped me choose new frames. He measured the distance between my pupils with a small ruler and told me the lenses would be ready in seven to ten business days.

Fatou Diallo had taken a home COVID test the evening before a family trip, and she set the timer on her phone for fifteen minutes as the instructions required. She placed the cassette on a paper towel on the bathroom counter and read the leaflet while she waited. The leaflet explained that a line next to the letter C meant the test was working, and a line next to the letter T meant a positive result. When the timer went off, there was a single line at C and no line at T. The result was negative. The instructions recommended a second test forty-eight hours later for the most reliable result, so Fatou wrote the time on the box with a marker. She put the used cassette and swab in the small plastic bag provided and threw it away. Then she packed the second test in her toiletry bag so she could take it on the second day of the trip.

My results from the sleep study arrived in the patient portal six days after I spent the night at the sleep center. The summary page reported an apnea-hypopnea index of eighteen events per hour, which the report classified as moderate obstructive sleep apnea. It also listed my lowest oxygen saturation during the night as eighty-six percent. The sleep physician, Dr. Abernathy, had recommended a trial of a CPAP machine and had sent an order to a medical equipment supplier. The supplier called me the following day to schedule a fitting. A respiratory therapist named Lorenzo Vitale met with me at their office and showed me three mask styles: a full face mask, a nasal mask, and nasal pillows. I tried each one on for a few minutes while the machine ran at a low pressure. I chose the nasal pillows. He set the machine to an automatic pressure range and showed me how to clean the tubing.

Mr. Halloran walked down the rows handing back the chemistry exams face down. Jun Takahashi turned his over and saw the score circled in red at the top: 82 out of 100. He flipped through the pages. He had lost six points on the stoichiometry problem because he had used the wrong molar mass for sulfuric acid, and four points on a short-answer question about Le Chatelier's principle where he had described the shift in the wrong direction. The rest of the deductions were single points for missing units. Mr. Halloran went to the board and worked through the stoichiometry problem step by step, writing each conversion on a new line. Jun corrected his work in pencil next to the original. At the end of class, the teacher said that students could submit written corrections for up to half of the lost points, due the following Monday, stapled to the original exam.

I got my history midterm back on Thursday. The grade was a B-plus, written at the top of the blue book next to the number 87. My teacher, Ms. Okonjo, had written comments in the margins of my essay on the causes of the First World War. She noted that my paragraph on the alliance system was well organized but that I needed more specific evidence for the section on militarism, such as naval spending figures. On the short-answer section, I had confused the dates of two treaties. She had underlined the error and written the correct year above it. At the end of the essay, she wrote a sentence suggesting I use the textbook's appendix of primary sources for the final paper. During class, she handed out a rubric for the final paper that broke the score into thesis, evidence, organization, and citations. I placed the rubric inside the front cover of my history binder.

Professor Antonescu returned the statistics exams at the start of the lecture, calling each student's name in alphabetical order. Kalani Akana went down to the front when she heard her name and took the stapled packet. Her score was 71 out of 90. She sat back down and looked at the breakdown on the cover sheet. The multiple-choice section was 28 out of 30. On the free-response section, she had lost the most points on the hypothesis testing problem, where she had used a one-tailed test when the question called for a two-tailed test. The grader had written the correct critical value next to her answer. The professor then put the class distribution on the projector: a mean of 66 and a standard deviation of eleven. He said the final exam would cover the same material plus regression. Kalani wrote the mean and standard deviation on the cover sheet and slid the exam into her folder.

The teacher put my spelling test on my desk when we came in from recess. I am in fourth grade, and the test had twenty words. My teacher, Mrs. Penhaligon, had marked each word with a check or a small line. I got seventeen right. The three I missed were necessary, which I spelled with two s's in the wrong place, separate, which I spelled with an e in the middle, and rhythm, which I spelled without the h. She had written each word correctly next to my version. On the back of the test, there was a stamp of a star and the number 17 out of 20. She told the class that we needed to write each missed word five times in our notebooks before Friday. I took out my notebook and wrote necessary five times, then separate, then rhythm. Then I put the test in my take-home folder for my dad to sign.

Ngozi Eze was a second-year law student, and her contracts exam had been graded anonymously, using a number instead of her name. The registrar posted the grades online by exam number, and the professor returned the exam booklets in the student services office. Ngozi picked hers up from a box sorted by number. Her grade was a B. The professor had written a short comment on the front page saying her issue spotting was thorough but that her analysis of consideration in the second fact pattern did not apply the bargained-for exchange test. Inside, there were checkmarks next to the issues she had identified and a few margin notes where the analysis was incomplete. The professor's office hours were on Wednesdays from two to four. Ngozi wrote the time in her planner and took the booklet to the library, where she compared her answer to the model answer the professor had posted on the course website.

My calculus exam came back during the last ten minutes of class. The score was 64 out of 80, which was eighty percent. I went through the problems one by one. On the related rates problem about the ladder sliding down the wall, I had set up the equation correctly but differentiated the wrong side, which cost me four points. On the integration by parts problem, I had made a sign error in the second step. Three other problems had full marks. The teacher, Mr. Castellanos, had written a short note at the bottom asking me to show my work more clearly on the limits section, since he could not follow one of my steps. He announced that a review session for the next unit would be held on Tuesday after school in Room 214. I put the exam into the folder for the class and wrote Room 214 and the date on the back of my hand so I would remember.

Thabo Molefe opened the email from his biology lecturer, which contained a link to the online grading platform. The practical exam on cell biology had been graded, and his mark was 34 out of 40. The feedback was split into sections. For the microscopy section, the marker had written that his drawing of onion epidermis cells was accurate and labeled correctly. For the data analysis section, he had calculated the mean correctly but had not included a standard deviation, which cost him three marks. For the short essay on osmosis, the marker noted that the explanation was correct but did not mention water potential, which cost him two marks. A final mark was deducted for a missing unit in a table. Thabo downloaded the feedback as a PDF and saved it in a folder named Biology Semester 2. He then opened the course schedule and checked the date of the next practical, which was in three weeks.

Mrs. Delgado handed back our English essays on a Friday afternoon. Mine was about the use of setting in a novel we had read for class, and it had a grade of 91 written in green ink at the top. She had used a rubric with five categories: thesis, evidence, analysis, organization, and mechanics. I had full marks in thesis and organization. Under evidence, she wrote that I had used good quotations but needed to include page numbers. Under mechanics, she circled three comma splices and wrote the term in the margin. On the last page, she wrote that my conclusion repeated the introduction too closely and suggested ending with a point about the author's choices. She also mentioned that the next essay, on character development, would be due in two weeks. I put the essay in my backpack and wrote the due date for the next essay in my planner, next to a note about page numbers.

The physics teacher, Mr. Banerjee, returned the unit test on circular motion and gravitation. Ilse Vandermeer received hers with a score of 45 out of 50. The test had five problems. She had made a single error, on the problem about orbital period, where she had forgotten to convert the radius from kilometers to meters. The answer was off by a factor of a thousand, and he had deducted five points for the error while giving credit for the method. Mr. Banerjee went over the most commonly missed problem on the board, which was not the one Ilse had missed. It was a problem about the tension in a string for an object moving in a vertical circle. He drew a free-body diagram at the top and the bottom of the circle and showed how the net force changed. Ilse took notes on the method in her notebook, under the heading Vertical Circles.

I took the driving theory exam at the licensing office, and the results came back on the computer screen immediately after I submitted the last answer. There were thirty-five questions, and I needed thirty to pass. My score was thirty-two. The screen listed the three questions I had missed: one about the minimum following distance in wet conditions, one about the meaning of a yellow diamond-shaped sign, and one about parking near a fire hydrant. The clerk at the counter, a woman named Rosaleen Doherty, printed my results and stamped the page with the office seal. She explained that I now needed to book the practical driving test, which had a waiting period of about five weeks. She gave me a sheet of paper with the booking website and a list of documents to bring. I folded the page and put it in my wallet, behind my student ID card.

Bongani Zulu was a graduate student, and his qualifying exam results came in the form of a letter from the department chair. The exam had been in two parts, a written portion in March and an oral portion in April. The letter stated that he had passed both parts and was now eligible to advance to candidacy. It listed the committee members who had evaluated the oral exam: Professors Rivera, Ostrowski, and Tanaka-Bell. Attached to the letter was a form that needed to be signed by his advisor and submitted to the graduate school within thirty days. It also mentioned that the dissertation proposal should be submitted by the end of the next semester. Bongani printed the form, filled in his student ID number and the date of the oral exam, and took it to his advisor's office on the fourth floor. His advisor signed it and wrote the date beside the signature.

My piano theory exam results came by mail in a large envelope from the music examination board. Inside was a certificate and a mark sheet. The exam had been graded out of 100, with 66 required to pass. I received 79. The mark sheet divided the score into sections: rhythm, pitch, keys and scales, intervals, chords, terms and signs, and the final section on a short musical extract. I had lost the most marks in the section on chords, where I had misidentified two cadences. The examiner had written a brief comment next to that section. The certificate had my name, the grade level, and the date of the exam printed on it, and it was signed by the chief examiner. My piano teacher, Mr. Ashworth-Mensah, asked me to bring the mark sheet to my next lesson so we could look at the chord section together before I started on the next level of theory.

Hollis Pemberton was in the cereal aisle comparing the unit prices on two boxes of oats when someone said his name. It was Amadou Traoré, who had lived across the hall from him in college. Amadou was pushing a cart with a case of sparkling water, a bag of onions, and several cans of chickpeas. They shook hands. Amadou said he had moved back to the area in January for a job at the water utility, where he worked on pipe replacement planning. Hollis said he was still at the same insurance company, now in the claims department on the second floor. They talked about the college dormitory, which had been torn down and replaced with a science building. Amadou took out his phone and they exchanged numbers. Hollis mentioned a pickup basketball game at the community center on Sunday mornings at nine. Amadou wrote down the address. Then they each continued down the aisle in opposite directions.

I was standing at the deli counter waiting for my number to be called when I recognized the woman next to me. It was Corinne Delacourt, a friend from high school I had not seen in about fifteen years. She was holding ticket number 48, and I had 49. We said hello and talked while the man behind the counter sliced a pound of turkey for someone else. She told me she worked as a pharmacist at a hospital two towns over and had two kids, eight and eleven. I told her I taught middle school science and lived near the old train station. She asked whether I still had the green bicycle I used to ride to school, and I told her I had sold it years ago. When her number was called, she ordered half a pound of provolone and a pound of ham. Before she left, she gave me her email address, and I typed it into my phone.

Two women reached for the same bunch of cilantro in the produce section, and one of them laughed and stepped back. It was Mei-Ling Chao, and the other was Rukhsana Begum. They had worked together at a bank branch about ten years earlier and had not been in contact since. They stood next to the herb display and talked for several minutes. Rukhsana said she had left the bank and now ran the books for a small construction firm. Mei-Ling said she was still in banking but had moved to the mortgage department at the head office downtown. They compared notes on former coworkers: one had retired, and another had moved to Vancouver. Rukhsana mentioned that the bank branch where they had worked was now a phone store. Mei-Ling took the cilantro, and Rukhsana took the next bunch. They agreed to meet for lunch the following Thursday at a noodle place near Mei-Ling's office.

I saw my old friend Dragan Petrović in the checkout line at the grocery store on Saturday morning. He was two people ahead of me, loading a bag of potatoes, a carton of eggs, and a large container of yogurt onto the conveyor belt. We had played in the same amateur football league for five years until I moved away for work. I waved, and he waited for me by the exit after paying. He told me he was coaching his son's under-twelve team now, and that the league had moved to a new set of fields by the river. He asked whether I still played. I told him I had joined a five-a-side league on Wednesday nights. We stood by the shopping carts and talked about some of the players we used to know, including the goalkeeper, who had become a firefighter. Dragan gave me the schedule for his son's games, which were on Sunday afternoons at two.

Sunniva Bakke was looking for a particular brand of rye crispbread when a man in a blue raincoat stopped beside her and asked whether she had gone to a summer sailing camp on the coast in the nineties. She said yes. He introduced himself as Leopold Wachter and said he had been in the same group as her for two summers. She remembered the name. He was now a structural engineer and lived in the neighborhood just north of the store. Sunniva said she worked for the regional ferry company in scheduling. Leopold mentioned that one of the camp instructors had written a book about sailing knots, and that he had a copy at home. They talked for a few more minutes about the camp's location, which had since been turned into a marine research station. Before they parted, Sunniva showed him where the crispbread was kept, on the bottom shelf near the end of the aisle.

The frozen food section was mostly empty on a weekday afternoon, which is why I noticed the man reading the nutrition label on a bag of frozen peas. It was Ezekiel Brandão, who had been my roommate during a summer internship in another city about twelve years before. I said his name, and he looked up. He said he lived about ten minutes away now, and that he had changed careers from accounting to working as a nurse in a pediatric clinic. I told him I was still in the same field, doing data analysis for a shipping company. He asked about the apartment we had shared, which had a balcony that faced a parking garage. We talked for a few minutes about the internship and the other people in the program. Then he picked up the bag of peas and a box of frozen dumplings, and we agreed to send each other a message later in the week to set up a time to get coffee.

Roberta Fontaine and Nasser Haddadin had been friends in a choir about twenty years ago. They ran into each other at the bakery counter of a grocery store on a Tuesday morning. Roberta was ordering a loaf of seeded rye, and Nasser was buying a dozen pita. They stood at the end of the counter and talked. Nasser explained that he had moved back from Dubai the previous year and was working as an architect for a firm that designed schools. Roberta said she was the director of a community music program at a library. She mentioned that the program ran a small choir on Monday evenings and that they needed more tenors. Nasser said he had not sung in a choir since they had both been members. Roberta wrote the address of the library on the back of the bakery receipt and handed it to him. She told him rehearsals started at seven and lasted ninety minutes.

I was weighing a bag of apples on the scale in the produce section when I heard someone say my name from behind me. It was Teodora Ilieva, who had been my lab partner in a chemistry course in my first year of university. She had a small basket with a block of cheese, a box of crackers, and two lemons. She said she was in town for a work trip and had stopped at the store to get food for the hotel room. She worked as a quality control chemist at a pharmaceutical plant on the other side of the country. I told her I had gone into environmental consulting. We spent a few minutes trying to remember the name of the professor who taught that chemistry course. Neither of us could recall it. She said she was flying out on Thursday morning. We traded phone numbers, and I recommended a restaurant near her hotel that served good fish.

Ezra Goldberg was in line at the pharmacy counter inside the grocery store when a woman behind him tapped his shoulder. It was Lakshmi Venkataraman. They had both worked as summer counselors at a day camp when they were teenagers. Lakshmi was waiting to pick up a prescription, and Ezra was dropping one off. They moved to the side so others could get to the counter and talked for about ten minutes. Lakshmi was now a civil engineer for the county and worked on bridge inspections. Ezra ran a small bookbinding shop in the arts district. Lakshmi asked about the camp, which had closed several years before, and Ezra said the property had been turned into a nature preserve with walking trails. Lakshmi said she had been to the preserve once but had not realized it was the same site. When the pharmacist called Ezra's name, he handed over his prescription and the two of them said goodbye.

On Sunday evening, I went to the grocery store to buy rice and a few vegetables for the week. In the canned goods aisle, I saw a man I recognized from my old neighborhood, where I had grown up. His name was Ignatius Mwangi, and we had walked to primary school together every morning for six years. He was reading the label on a can of coconut milk. I said hello, and he recognized me after a moment. He said he had moved to this side of the city two years earlier for a job as a bus mechanic at the depot on Fifth Street. I told him I worked at the post office sorting facility. He asked whether my parents still lived in the old house, and I told him they did. We talked about the school, which had added a new wing. Then he took two cans of coconut milk and put them in his cart, and I continued on to the rice aisle.

Marguerite Lacroix stopped her cart at the end of the dairy aisle when she saw a man she knew reaching for a carton of milk. It was Siddharth Iyer, who had lived next door to her family when they were both children. He recognized her right away. They talked about the street where they had grown up. Siddharth said his parents had sold the house about five years ago, and that the new owners had added a second floor. Marguerite said her mother still lived in the same house and walked to the corner store every morning. Siddharth was now a high school chemistry teacher. Marguerite worked as a court stenographer. He asked whether she still had the dog she used to walk down the block, and she explained that the dog had died years ago and that her mother now had a cat. They stood there for a few minutes more, then exchanged email addresses and continued their shopping.

I went to the grocery store on my lunch break to pick up a salad, and in the line at the self-checkout, I ran into an old friend, Casimir Nowak. We had been on the same debate team in high school and had traveled to tournaments together on weekends. He was holding a sandwich and a bottle of iced tea. He told me he worked as a paralegal at a law firm in the office building across the street. I told him I worked for the city, in the transportation planning department, three blocks away. We both scanned our items and paid, then walked out together. On the sidewalk, he mentioned that our old debate coach was retiring at the end of the year and that the school was holding a small event in her honor in June. He said he would forward me the email invitation. I gave him my work email, and he typed it into his phone before crossing at the light.

Victor Almeida was driving on the highway to his office when the temperature gauge on the dashboard climbed into the red. He turned on his hazard lights, signaled, and moved onto the shoulder. He shut off the engine and waited a few minutes before opening the hood, as the manual advised. Steam was coming from the area near the radiator cap. He did not open it. He called his roadside assistance number, which was printed on a card in his wallet. The operator asked for his location, and Victor read the mile marker from a green sign about fifty meters ahead. The operator said a tow truck would arrive in about forty minutes. Victor then called his manager and said he would be late. The tow truck arrived after thirty-five minutes. The driver connected the car to the winch, pulled it onto the flatbed, and gave Victor a ride to the repair shop, which was about six kilometers away.

My car stopped running at a traffic light about two kilometers from my office. The engine turned off, and when I turned the key, the dashboard lights came on but the starter only clicked. I put the car in neutral and pushed the button for the hazard lights. A man in a delivery van pulled up behind me and offered to help push the car to the side of the road. We pushed it into a parking spot by a bus stop. I called a mobile mechanic I had used before, Ignacio Barros, who said he could be there in twenty minutes. When he arrived, he tested the battery with a small handheld meter, which showed 11.2 volts. He said the battery was too low to start the engine and that it was five years old. He had a replacement battery in his van. He installed it, tested the charging system, and printed an invoice from a portable printer. The total was one hundred and sixty dollars.

Ji-woo Kang's car began to make a grinding noise from the front left wheel on her drive to work. The noise got louder each time she pressed the brake. She pulled into the parking lot of a gas station and called the dealership's service department. The service advisor, a man named Eamon Gallagher, said it was likely the brake pads had worn down to the metal backing plates, and that she should not drive it more than necessary. He offered to send a tow truck, which was covered under her extended warranty. While she waited, Ji-woo bought a coffee inside the gas station and emailed her supervisor to say she would work from the dealership's waiting room. The tow truck arrived after about thirty minutes. At the dealership, the technician confirmed that both front pads and one rotor needed replacement. Eamon gave her an estimate of two hours for the repair, and she set up her laptop at a table in the waiting area.

I was on a two-lane road heading toward the bridge when the car lost power and the steering became heavy. The engine had stalled. I steered onto the gravel shoulder and stopped. When I tried to restart it, the engine turned over several times but did not catch. I checked the fuel gauge, which showed about a quarter of a tank. I opened the hood, though I did not see anything out of place. I called the towing company listed on my insurance card. The dispatcher took my location and my license plate number and said a driver would arrive within an hour. While waiting, I sent a message to my coworker, Ottilie Brandstrom, to ask her to cover the morning shift meeting. The tow truck driver arrived and tried to jump-start the car, but it still would not start. He loaded it onto the truck and took it to a garage near my house, where the mechanic said he would look at the fuel pump.

Kofi Mensah's car had a flat tire on the way to work. He noticed the steering pulling to the right and then heard a rhythmic thumping. He pulled off at the next exit and stopped in the parking lot of a closed restaurant. The rear passenger side tire was flat, and there was a screw embedded in the tread. He opened the trunk and took out the spare tire, the jack, and the lug wrench. He loosened the lug nuts a half turn each before raising the car, as he had been taught. Then he positioned the jack under the reinforced point near the rear wheel and raised the car until the tire was off the ground. He removed the nuts and the flat tire and mounted the spare. After tightening the nuts in a star pattern, he lowered the car. The whole process took about twenty-five minutes. He drove to a tire shop near his office, where they patched the original tire for twenty dollars.

The check engine light came on while I was merging onto the freeway, and about a minute later the car started losing speed. I pulled into the right lane and then onto the shoulder. The engine was still running, but it was shaking. I turned it off and called my husband, Anselm, who was at home with our daughter. He looked up the nearest auto repair shop on his computer and gave me the phone number. The shop could not send a tow truck, so I called the motor club, which arranged one. I waited in the car with my seatbelt on, as the motor club advised, and read the owner's manual section on warning lights. The tow driver arrived after fifty minutes and took the car to the shop. The mechanic connected a diagnostic scanner to the port under the dashboard. It showed a misfire in cylinder three, and he said it was likely a failed ignition coil.

Constance Mbeki's car stopped working in the left-turn lane of a busy intersection during the morning commute. The dashboard displayed a message about the transmission. She turned on the hazard lights and called the non-emergency police line, as the lane was blocking traffic. An officer arrived about ten minutes later and parked behind her car with the patrol lights flashing. He helped direct traffic around her until the tow truck arrived. The tow truck driver lifted the front of the car with the wheel lift and pulled it across the intersection to a parking lot. He said the transmission might have overheated and suggested taking it to a specialist. Rosalind gave him the address of a transmission shop her brother had used. She rode in the cab of the tow truck to the shop and then took a bus from a stop across the street to her office, which was four stops away.

I drive an old pickup truck to my job at the lumber yard, and on Wednesday it would not start in my driveway. I tried several times. The engine turned over but did not fire. I checked the obvious things first. The fuel gauge was at half, and the battery terminals were tight and clean. I called my neighbor, Bartholomew Udeh, who is a retired mechanic. He came over with a toolbox and a spray can of starting fluid. He sprayed a short burst into the air intake and asked me to try again. The engine started for a few seconds and then died. He said that meant the fuel was probably not getting to the engine, and that the fuel filter or fuel pump was the likely problem. He offered to replace the filter that afternoon if I bought the part. I called my supervisor to say I would be late and drove his car to the auto parts store to get the filter.

Mikhail Sorokin was halfway to work when a warning light shaped like an oil can appeared on the dashboard. He turned off the radio and pulled into the next rest area. He checked the oil level with the dipstick and found it barely touched the bottom mark. The car had been due for an oil change two weeks before. He walked to the convenience store at the rest area and bought two quarts of the correct grade of oil, which he found by checking the label inside the hood. He added one quart, checked the dipstick again, and added half of the second. The level reached the middle of the range. The warning light went off when he restarted the engine. He continued to work and called a quick-lube shop from his office to schedule an oil change for that afternoon. The receptionist, Paloma Ruiz, asked for the make and model and gave him a slot at four.

My car's alternator failed on the drive to the train station. I noticed the headlights getting dimmer and the radio cutting out, and then the battery light came on. I kept driving because the station was only about a kilometer away, but the engine stopped in the parking lot before I could reach a space. I pushed the car to the edge of the lot with help from a man named Tobias Hallberg who was walking to the same train. I left the car there and caught the train to work. During my lunch break, I called a garage near the station and arranged for them to tow the car. The mechanic, a woman named Henrietta Osei, called me later that afternoon and explained that the alternator had worn out and was no longer charging the battery. She quoted a price for a rebuilt alternator, including labor, and said the car would be ready by noon the next day.

Dolores Arriaga's car began to steam from under the hood as she drove up a hill on her way to the hospital where she worked. She pulled into the parking lot of a hardware store at the top of the hill and turned off the engine. She called the hospital's staffing office and told the coordinator that she would arrive late for her shift. Then she called a tow company. The dispatcher said the wait would be about an hour. Dolores went into the hardware store and bought a gallon jug of distilled water. After the engine had cooled for forty-five minutes, she opened the hood, located the coolant reservoir, and noticed the level was below the minimum line. She also saw a small crack in the upper radiator hose. The tow truck arrived, and the driver agreed that the hose was the cause. He took the car to a repair shop on the main road, and Dolores called a taxi to the hospital.

On the way to my job at the school, my car's clutch pedal went to the floor and stayed there. I could not shift out of second gear. I drove slowly in second gear for a few blocks and stopped in the parking lot of a church. I called my car insurance company, and the representative arranged a tow. While I waited, I sent an email to the school's office manager, Gertrude Pfeiffer, explaining that I would be about an hour late and asking whether someone could cover my first-period class. The tow truck driver arrived in about thirty-five minutes. He looked at the clutch pedal and said it was likely a hydraulic problem, possibly a leak in the clutch master cylinder. He loaded the car and took it to a garage that specialized in manual transmissions. The garage gave me a ride to the school in their courtesy van, and the driver dropped me off at the front entrance at 9:15.

Patrice Durand-Hart sat at the kitchen table at 11:40 on Friday night with a cup of chamomile tea and the newspaper crossword. Her sixteen-year-old son, Elias, had gone to a friend's birthday party and had a midnight curfew. The friend's mother had texted earlier in the evening to say that the party was ending at 11:30 and that she would drive Elias and two other boys home. Patrice had filled in about half of the crossword. At 11:52, she heard a car door outside and the sound of the garage keypad. Elias came in through the side door carrying a paper plate with two slices of cake wrapped in foil. He said the party had been at a bowling alley and then at the house. He put the cake in the refrigerator and asked whether he could sleep in the next morning. Patrice said yes, as long as he mowed the lawn by two in the afternoon.

I stayed up on Saturday night to wait for my daughter, Anouk, who was seventeen and had driven to a concert in the city with two friends. Our agreement was that she would text me when the concert ended and again when she left the parking garage. The first text came at 10:48: the show was over. The second came at 11:15: leaving the garage now. The drive from the city usually took about fifty minutes. I folded laundry in the living room and watched part of a documentary about glaciers. At 12:10, I heard the car in the driveway. She came in and put the car keys on the hook by the door. She said the parking garage had a long line to exit and that traffic on the bridge had been slow because of construction. I asked whether she had eaten, and she said they had stopped for burritos. She went upstairs, and I turned off the lights in the living room.

Kwame Owusu-Ansah looked at the clock on the stove, which read 12:20. His daughter, Akosua, had told him she would be home by midnight after working the closing shift at the movie theater. The theater closed at 11:30, and cleanup usually took about half an hour. He picked up his phone and checked the location-sharing app the family used. It showed her phone still at the theater. He sent her a text asking for an update. She replied a minute later: the manager had asked her to stay to count the concession stand drawer because another employee had left early. She expected to be done in fifteen minutes. Kwame wrote back that he would leave the porch light on. He washed the few dishes in the sink and wiped down the counter. At 12:48, the app showed her moving, and at 1:01 she pulled into the driveway. She came in with her uniform shirt over her arm.

My son, Rory, was out with his friends on a Friday night, and his curfew was eleven. I was reading in the armchair by the front window with the lamp on. At 10:45, I got a text from him saying he was at Callum's house and would be home in twenty minutes. Callum lived about a mile and a half away, and Rory had ridden his bicycle. I checked the weather app, which said it was clear and about nine degrees. I went to the kitchen and made a cup of tea. At 11:03, I saw his bicycle light come around the corner at the end of the street. He rode up the driveway, put the bicycle in the garage, and came in through the back door. He said they had been playing a video game and eating pizza. I reminded him he had a dentist appointment at nine the next morning, and he set an alarm on his phone before going upstairs.

Svetlana Ivanova's daughter, Daria, was fifteen and had gone to a school dance at the gymnasium. The dance ended at ten, and a parent from another family, Mr. Grantham, had arranged to drive three of the girls home. Svetlana sat on the couch with her laptop and worked on a presentation for a meeting the next week. At 10:15, she got a text from Daria saying they were leaving the school. The ride home was about fifteen minutes, but the car would make two other stops first. Svetlana finished the slides on quarterly budget figures and saved the file. At 10:42, she heard a car pull up outside and saw headlights through the front curtains. Daria came in, took off her shoes at the door, and said that the dance had a photo booth and a table with snacks. Svetlana closed the laptop and turned off the television, which had been playing a cooking program on low volume.

I waited up for my son, Mateus, on the night he took the car to his first late shift at the grocery store where he stocks shelves. He was seventeen and had had his license for four months. The shift ended at eleven, and the drive home was about ten minutes on local roads. I sat at the dining table and paid bills online: the electricity, the water, and the internet. At 11:12, I received a text from him that said, leaving now. At 11:25, I heard the car turn into the driveway and the engine turn off. He came inside carrying a box of cereal and a gallon of milk, which I had asked him to buy with the family card. He set them on the counter and handed me the receipt. He said that the store had received a large delivery of canned goods and that he had spent most of the shift in aisle six. He went upstairs to shower, and I locked the front door.

Lionel Oduya-Price had agreed to let his daughter, Imani, attend a sleepover at a friend's house, but the plan changed at nine in the evening when the friend's family had a power outage. The friend's father called Lionel to say the girls would watch a movie at a neighbor's house and that he would drive Imani home around midnight instead. Lionel stayed up in the living room. He watched a football match that had been recorded earlier in the day and then started on a puzzle book. At 11:50, he received a text from the friend's father saying they were on the way. The drive took about twenty minutes. Lionel turned on the porch light and unlocked the front door. When the car arrived, Imani got out with her sleeping bag and a backpack. The friend's father waved from the driver's seat. Imani said the power had come back on just as they were leaving. Lionel thanked the father and closed the door.

I was waiting up for my daughter, Freya, who was out at a friend's graduation party on the other side of town. Her curfew was one o'clock, extended for the occasion. Her friend's older brother was giving her a ride home. At 12:30, I was watching an old film in the den with the volume low. I had my phone on the armrest. At 12:51, she sent a message saying they were five minutes away. I paused the film and went to the kitchen to put away the dishes from the dish rack. I heard a car stop in front of the house a little after one. Freya came in and hung her jacket on the hook. She said the party had a barbecue in the backyard and that the friend's family had set up a projector on the garage wall to show photos from the school year. I asked whether she had her house key, and she showed it to me on her keychain.

Hiroshi Watanabe sat at the kitchen table with a stack of receipts and a calculator, sorting expenses for the family's tax return. It was 11:30, and his son, Kaito, who was eighteen, was due home from a late shift at the restaurant where he washed dishes. Kaito usually took the last bus, which left a stop near the restaurant at 11:20 and arrived at the stop on their street at 11:42. Hiroshi entered the totals into a spreadsheet on his laptop: medical receipts, charitable donations, and home office supplies. At 11:46, he heard the front gate latch and then the key in the lock. Kaito came in and placed his work shoes on the mat by the door. He said the bus had been on time and that the restaurant had been busy because of a large reservation. Hiroshi asked him to wake up early to help move a dresser on Saturday morning, and Kaito agreed before going to bed.
