My stepdaughter, Valentina, had gone to a friend's house to study for a final exam, and she had told me she would be back by eleven. I sat on the front porch with a book and a flashlight because the night was warm and the inside of the house was still holding the heat from the afternoon. Around 10:45, I got a text from her saying that they had decided to finish the last chapter and that she would be back at 11:30. I replied with okay and kept reading. A neighbor, Wilhelmina Strauss, walked by with her dog and stopped to say good evening. We talked for a few minutes about the street repaving scheduled for the next month. At 11:34, I saw Valentina walking down the sidewalk with her backpack. She came up the steps and said the exam was on Monday at eight. I picked up my book and the flashlight and followed her inside.

Adaeze Nwosu checked the time on the microwave clock: 1:05 in the morning. Her son, Chinedu, nineteen and home from university for the summer, had gone out with friends and said he would be home around one. He had taken the car. Adaeze was in the living room folding a stack of towels from the dryer. She sent him a short text, asking whether he was on his way. He replied that he was dropping off a friend in the next neighborhood and would be home in ten minutes. Adaeze finished folding the towels and carried them up to the linen closet. She came back down and filled a glass of water in the kitchen. At 1:18, she saw the headlights through the front window. Chinedu parked the car and came inside. He set the car keys and a parking garage receipt on the counter. He said they had gone to a jazz club and that the parking had been expensive.

I waited up for my son, Yaroslav, on the night he came back from a school trip to the capital. The bus was scheduled to arrive at the school parking lot at 11:00, and parents were supposed to pick up their children there. At 10:30, the school sent an automated text saying the bus would arrive at 11:45 because of traffic on the highway. I stayed at home until 11:25 and then drove to the school. There were already about a dozen cars in the lot, with their engines running and the headlights on. A teacher, Mr. Fairweather, stood near the entrance with a clipboard. The bus arrived at 11:50. Students got off one at a time, and the teacher checked off each name on his list. Yaroslav came out with a duffel bag and a paper bag of souvenirs. He told me the group had visited the parliament building and two museums. We drove home, and he went straight to bed.

At 2:30 on Tuesday, Wendell Osterhout received a calendar invitation from his manager, Farida Rahimi, titled Quick check-in, for 3:00 in her office. He finished the invoice he was processing, saved the spreadsheet, and walked down the hall. Farida's office had a small round table with two chairs, and she gestured to one of them. She explained that the accounts payable team was moving to a new software system in the next quarter and that she wanted Wendell to be one of three people trained first. The training would be four half-day sessions, held in the conference room on the second floor, beginning on the eighth. After that, he would help train the other members of the team. She handed him a printed schedule and a login for the software's practice environment. Wendell asked whether his regular invoice load would be reduced during the training weeks. Farida said she would assign part of it to a temporary employee.

My manager, Leandro Saldívar, sent me a message on the company chat asking me to stop by his office before lunch. I finished updating a shipping manifest and walked over at 11:40. He was on the phone, so I waited outside the door until he waved me in. He said the warehouse was changing its shift structure in January, from two eight-hour shifts to three, and he wanted to know which shift I would prefer. The options were six to two, two to ten, and ten to six. He explained that shift preference would be assigned by seniority, and that I was fourth on the list among the inventory clerks. I told him I preferred the six-to-two shift, since I take a class on Tuesday evenings. He wrote my name next to that shift on a printed sheet. He also said the new schedule would be posted on the break room board by the fifteenth of December.

Ottoline Rasmussen was called into her manager's office on a Thursday morning. Her manager, a man named Gideon Thorvaldsen, had a laptop open on the desk and turned it toward her. On the screen was the floor plan for the office, which was being reorganized. He explained that the marketing team would be moving from the third floor to the fifth floor at the end of the month, into a space with an open layout and two meeting rooms. He pointed to a desk near the window and said it would be hers. Each employee would receive four moving boxes and a set of labels, and the facilities team would move the boxes on a Friday evening. Personal items needed to be packed by noon that day. Ottoline asked whether her monitor stand and keyboard would be moved as well. Gideon said all equipment would be moved by the facilities team and set up by Monday morning.

My supervisor at the hospital, a nurse manager named Philippa Adebanjo, asked me to come to her office at the end of my shift. I clocked out at 7:15 in the evening and went to the small office next to the nurses' station. She told me that the unit was updating its procedure for medication reconciliation at patient discharge, and that every nurse needed to complete an online training module before the end of the month. She also said the hospital was looking for two nurses from our floor to serve on a committee that would review the procedure over the next six months. The committee would meet once every two weeks for an hour, and the time would count as paid hours. I said I would be willing to join. She wrote my name on a list and told me the first meeting would be on the twenty-first, in conference room B on the ground floor, at 3:00.

Ramón Escobedo had been working at the call center for eleven months when his manager, Ilona Szabo, called him into her office. She said she had been reviewing call metrics and wanted to go over his numbers with him. She pulled up a dashboard on her monitor. His average call handling time was six minutes and twenty seconds, slightly below the team target of seven minutes. His first-call resolution rate was eighty-one percent, which met the target. She noted that his after-call work time was longer than average, at about ninety seconds per call, and asked how he entered his notes. Ramón explained that he typed full sentences in the notes field. Ilona showed him a set of standard abbreviations that the team used for common issues, which were saved in a shared document. She sent him the link and suggested that he try using them for a week. They scheduled a follow-up meeting in two weeks to review the numbers again.

I was asked to come into my manager's office on a Monday afternoon, and when I sat down, she slid a printed document across the desk. My manager, Cordelia Mbatha, explained that the company was renewing its health insurance contract and that the benefits enrollment period would open the following week. The document listed three plans with their monthly premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket maximums. She explained that the human resources department had asked managers to deliver the packets in person so that each employee would have a chance to ask questions. She pointed out that the plan I was currently on would have a slightly higher premium, by about twelve dollars per paycheck, but the deductible would stay the same. I asked about the dental coverage, and she showed me a separate page with the dental plan options. She told me that the deadline for enrollment was the thirtieth and that the forms could be submitted online through the employee portal.

Darius Farahani worked as a cashier at a hardware store. On Saturday, the store manager, Agnieszka Wróbel, asked him to come to the back office during his break. The office had a desk, a filing cabinet, and a safe. She explained that the store was promoting one of the cashiers to a key holder position, which involved opening the store on weekends and counting the cash drawers at closing. She asked whether he would be interested. The position came with a raise of one dollar and fifty cents per hour. She explained that he would need to complete a training on the alarm system and the safe procedures, which would take two shifts. Darius asked about the opening time, and she said it was 6:30 on Saturdays and 7:30 on Sundays. He said he was interested. She gave him a form to sign and told him the training would start the following weekend with the assistant manager.

On Wednesday, my department head, Professor Lukas Brenneman, asked me to come by his office at the university. I work as an administrative coordinator for the geology department. He told me that the department was hosting an external review in the spring, in which a panel of three professors from other universities would visit for two days. He asked me to handle the logistics: booking hotel rooms, arranging meals, reserving rooms for meetings, and preparing a printed binder for each reviewer. He handed me a list of the reviewers' names and their institutions. He also gave me a draft agenda, which included a tour of the rock preparation lab and meetings with graduate students. I asked about the budget for the visit, and he said the dean's office had approved four thousand dollars. I took notes in my notebook and said I would send him a draft schedule by the end of the following week.

Fiona MacAllister was a junior engineer at a firm that designed water treatment plants. Her manager, Bjørn Haugland, called her into his office on a Friday morning. He said the firm had won a contract for a project in a town about two hours north, and that he wanted her to be part of the site team. The project would involve weekly visits to the site for about six months, usually on Tuesdays. Mileage would be reimbursed, and a company car was available if she preferred. He explained that her role would be to document the construction progress, take photos, and record measurements to compare with the design drawings. He handed her a binder with the project specifications. Fiona asked whether she would need any additional safety training. Bjørn said she would need to complete a confined space entry course, which the firm would schedule for her the following month. She took the binder back to her desk and started reading the first section.

My manager called me into her office to discuss my upcoming annual review. Her name was Esperanza Villalobos, and she had a printed copy of the self-evaluation form I had submitted two weeks before. She went through each section of the form. In the section on goals, she noted that I had completed three of the four goals we had set the previous year. The fourth goal, which was to finish a certification course in project management, was still in progress. She asked about my timeline, and I said I expected to complete the last module by March. She said that the company would reimburse the course fee once I submitted the certificate. In the section on next year's goals, she suggested adding a goal related to mentoring a new hire who would join the team in February. I agreed. She said the formal review meeting would be scheduled for the following week, and she would send a calendar invitation.

Obinna Chukwu worked at a printing company, operating a large-format press. His supervisor, Hortensia Velásquez, asked him to come into her office near the loading dock. She told him that a new press had been ordered and would be delivered in five weeks. The manufacturer would send a technician to install it and train two operators. She wanted Obinna to be one of them because he had the most experience with the current machine. The training would take three full days, and during that time another operator would cover his shifts on the old press. She showed him the specification sheet for the new machine, which could print on sheets up to sixty-four inches wide and used a different type of ink. Obinna read the sheet and asked whether the current print queue would need to be adjusted during the installation week. Hortensia said she was already working on a revised schedule with the production planner and would share it on Monday.

My manager, Augustin Rousseau, called me into his office on a Thursday afternoon to talk about the company's new remote work policy. He handed me a two-page document from human resources. It said that employees in my role could now work from home two days a week, with Tuesdays and Thursdays as the required in-office days for everyone. He explained that each employee needed to fill out a form choosing their two remote days and confirming that they had a suitable work area at home with a reliable internet connection. The company would provide a second monitor, a keyboard, and a headset for home use if requested. I chose Mondays and Fridays as my remote days. He asked me to submit the form through the human resources portal by the end of the following week. He also mentioned that the equipment would be shipped to my home address within ten business days.

Harriet Blackwood spent the morning clearing out the attic of the house she had bought in the spring. The previous owners had left behind several cardboard boxes, a broken lamp, and a wooden trunk under the eaves. Inside the trunk, beneath a folded quilt, was a bundle of envelopes tied with string. The top envelope was addressed to a Mr. Edmund Whitlock at this house, with a postmark from 1952. Harriet untied the string and opened the first letter. It was two pages, written in blue ink, from someone who signed as Cousin Ada. The letter described the price of wheat, a new barn being built on a farm in Saskatchewan, and the weather during harvest. Harriet read the rest of the bundle, which contained eleven letters in total. She placed them in a plastic sleeve and called the local historical society. A volunteer named Lorcan Duffy said they would take the letters for their archive.

I was cleaning out my parents' attic with my brother when I found a shoebox labeled Letters in black marker. Inside were several envelopes, most of them addressed to my mother before she was married, at an address in a city where she had lived as a student. One envelope was different. It was addressed to my father and had a stamp from Chile. The letter inside was from a man named Ernesto Cifuentes, who had been my father's colleague at a mining company in the 1970s. It was three pages long, typed on thin paper. It described a project to build a road to a copper mine, with figures for the length of the road and the number of trucks used. It ended with a request for some technical drawings. I showed it to my brother, and we put it in a separate folder to give to our father, who was living in an apartment downtown.

Teresa Zielińska climbed into the attic of her house in late October to retrieve the box of winter clothes. While moving it, she knocked over a stack of old magazines, and a single envelope slid out from between two of them. It was addressed to her grandmother, who had lived in the house until the 1990s. The return address was a parish office in Kraków. The letter was in Polish, written in neat handwriting. Teresa read it slowly, since her Polish was from childhood lessons. It confirmed the date and location of her great-grandparents' wedding, which had taken place in 1923, and enclosed a copy of the parish record. The copy was still in the envelope, folded in thirds. It listed both names, the names of the witnesses, and the priest. Teresa took the envelope downstairs and scanned both pages on her printer. She uploaded the scans to the family genealogy website her cousin maintained.

I found the letter while I was emptying the attic before selling my house. It was inside a hardback copy of a gardening book from the 1960s. The envelope was addressed to the woman who had owned the house before me, a Mrs. Winifred Parry, according to the name on the envelope. The letter was from the city's parks department and was dated 1971. It confirmed her application to plant two oak trees in the strip of land between the sidewalk and the street in front of the house. It specified the species, red oak, and stated that the department would provide the saplings and plant them in the spring. I went outside and looked at the two large oak trees in front of the house. They were in the exact positions described in the letter. I took a photo of the letter and the trees and included both in the folder of documents I was preparing for the buyers.

Mustafa Aydın and his wife were clearing out the attic of their rented house before moving. In the corner, behind a pile of old insulation, Mustafa found a metal box with a hinged lid. Inside the box was a single letter in an envelope with no stamp. It was addressed to whoever lives here next and was signed by a man named Ambrose Kettering, dated 1984. The letter explained that Ambrose had built the shelving in the basement and the cabinet under the stairs. It included instructions for adjusting the shelf brackets and a note that the well pump in the backyard had been disconnected in 1979, when the house was connected to the city water supply. It also gave the depth of the old well, about sixty feet. Mustafa read it out loud to his wife. They agreed to leave the letter in the metal box in the attic for the next tenants and to send a copy to the landlord.

I found an old letter in my grandparents' attic while I was helping them prepare for a move to a smaller house. It was in a filing box labeled Taxes 1958 to 1965, mixed in with receipts and bank statements. The letter was from a company that had once made sewing machines and was addressed to my grandmother. It confirmed that her sewing machine had been repaired under warranty and listed the parts that had been replaced: a bobbin case, a needle plate, and a drive belt. The letter included the serial number of the machine. I went downstairs and found the same machine in the spare bedroom, covered with a cloth. The serial number on the metal plate matched the one in the letter. I showed the letter to my grandmother, who said she had used the machine to make all of my mother's school clothes. We put the letter in the drawer of the sewing machine cabinet.

Clement Abara was clearing the attic of a house he had inherited from an uncle, sorting items into three piles: keep, donate, and discard. Under a stack of old curtain rods, he found a manila envelope containing a typed letter. The letter was from a builder and was dated 1966. It described the construction of the house's addition, a two-room extension on the back, and listed the dimensions of each room, the materials used for the foundation, and the type of roofing. It also included the total cost of the project, which was four thousand two hundred dollars. Attached to the letter with a paper clip was a carbon copy of the building permit. Clement placed the letter in the keep pile. He later took it to the city's building department, where a clerk named Persephone Gialamas checked it against the records. She confirmed that the permit was on file and made a photocopy for the department's archive.

I was in the attic looking for a box of old photographs when I found a letter tucked inside a wooden picture frame. The frame held a photo of a schoolhouse, and the letter had been placed behind the cardboard backing. It was from the school's principal and addressed to my great-uncle, Lazarus Fenwick, who had been a teacher there. The letter was dated 1938 and was about his teaching assignment for the coming year. He would teach grades three through five in one classroom, with an enrollment of twenty-four students. The letter listed the subjects he was expected to cover: arithmetic, reading, penmanship, and geography. It also noted his annual salary and the date school would begin, the first Tuesday in September. I compared the schoolhouse in the photo with an image I found online of a schoolhouse that was now part of a county museum. They looked the same, down to the bell tower on the roof.

Yolanda Restrepo was helping her aunt clean out the attic of a farmhouse when she found a letter in the pocket of an old wool coat. The coat was hanging on a nail near the chimney. The letter was folded twice and had been written on a sheet of lined paper. It was from a man who signed his name as Horace and was addressed to someone named Marion. It described the delivery of a new tractor to the farm, the price of fuel, and the plan to plant corn on the north field that spring. There was no year on the letter, only the date March 14. Yolanda showed it to her aunt, who said that Horace and Marion had been the names of her own grandparents. The aunt took the letter and placed it in a photo album on the shelf in the living room, next to a picture of the farmhouse taken from the road.

I was cleaning the attic of my apartment building, which the tenants share for storage, when I found an envelope wedged between two floorboards. The building superintendent, Cornelius Vandenberg, had asked a few of us to help clear the space before the inspection. The envelope was addressed to a tenant in apartment 3B, a name I did not recognize, and was postmarked 1997. The letter was from a library and informed the tenant that three books were overdue. It listed the titles: a book on the history of railways, a novel, and a guide to bird watching. It also listed the fine, which was two dollars and forty cents. I showed it to Cornelius, who checked an old tenant list he kept in his office. The tenant had moved out in 1999. Cornelius put the letter in a folder with other items found in the attic, which he planned to give to the building's management company.

Ingrid Sundqvist had hired a company to insulate the attic of her house, and before the work could begin she needed to clear everything out. She brought down several boxes of holiday decorations, a set of old suitcases, and a cardboard file box. In the file box, under a stack of old utility bills, was a letter addressed to her father. It was from a ship's captain and was dated 1961. The letter confirmed her father's position as an apprentice engineer aboard a cargo ship sailing between Gothenburg and Montreal. It gave the date of departure, the name of the ship, and the wage he would receive per month. It also asked him to bring two sets of work clothes and his seaman's book. Ingrid placed the letter in a clear folder and put it in her desk drawer. Then she continued carrying boxes down so the attic would be empty when the crew arrived on Monday.

I went up to the attic on a Saturday to find the tent for a camping trip. The attic had not been cleaned out in years. Behind the tent bag, inside a plastic storage bin, I found a stack of envelopes. Most were Christmas cards, but one was a letter addressed to me, written by my own hand, with a note on the envelope: open in ten years. I remembered that my seventh-grade teacher, Mr. Okwuosa, had asked our class to write letters to our future selves. The letter was dated sixteen years earlier. In it, I had listed my height, which was four feet eleven, my favorite books, and the name of my best friend at the time, Henriette Moreau. I had also written down a prediction that by now I would own a car and live in another country. I own a car but still live in the same city. I put the letter back in the bin and carried the tent downstairs.
